\section[namorar]{namorar — to date, to go out with}

\label{lesson:PT-C491-namorar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to sweat, then the Portuguese for massage.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: namorar}
\textbf{namorar} — \textquotedblleft{}to date, to go out with\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A minha prima namora com um colega da faculdade.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My cousin is going out with a classmate from university.}
\end{quote}

In Portugal \emph{namorar com alguém}; in Brazil \emph{namorar alguém}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{namorar} is usually explained as a shortening of Old Portuguese \emph{enamorar} \textquotedblleft{}to make fall in love\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{amor} \textquotedblleft{}love\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{amor} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{namorar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{namorar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{namorar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to sweat, then the Portuguese for massage, then say \emph{namorar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does namorar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To date, to go out with\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o namoro]{o namoro — relationship (between a couple who are dating)}

\label{lesson:PT-C491-namoro}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for massage, then the Portuguese for to date.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o namoro}
\textbf{o namoro} — \textquotedblleft{}relationship (between a couple who are dating)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O namoro deles durou cinco anos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Their relationship lasted five years.}
\end{quote}

The boyfriend is \emph{o namorado}, the girlfriend \emph{a namorada}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{namoro} comes from \emph{namorar} \textquotedblleft{}to date\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{amor} \textquotedblleft{}love\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{amor} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[a paixão]{a paixão — passion}

\label{lesson:PT-C491-paixao}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to date, then the Portuguese for relationship.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a paixão}
\textbf{a paixão} — \textquotedblleft{}passion\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A música é a grande paixão do meu pai.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Music is my father's great passion.}
\end{quote}

Also strong love: \emph{uma paixão de verão} — a summer romance.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{paixão} is inherited, through Old Portuguese \emph{paixon}, from Late Latin \emph{passiō} \textquotedblleft{}suffering\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{patī} \textquotedblleft{}to suffer\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a paixão}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a paixão}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a paixão}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to date, then the Portuguese for relationship, then say \emph{a paixão} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a paixão mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Passion\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[apaixonar]{apaixonar — to fall in love (apaixonar-se por)}

\label{lesson:PT-C491-apaixonar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for relationship, then the Portuguese for passion.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: apaixonar}
\textbf{apaixonar} — \textquotedblleft{}to fall in love (apaixonar-se por)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O meu irmão apaixonou-se pela vizinha do lado.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My brother fell in love with the girl next door.}
\end{quote}

Reflexive in practice: \emph{apaixonar-se por alguém}. \emph{Estar apaixonado} — to be in love.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{apaixonar} is built from \emph{a-} and \emph{paixão} \textquotedblleft{}passion\textquotedblright{}, which goes back to Late Latin \emph{passiō} \textquotedblleft{}suffering\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[abraçar]{abraçar — to hug, to embrace}

\label{lesson:PT-C491-abracar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for passion, then the Portuguese for to fall in love.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: abraçar}
\textbf{abraçar} — \textquotedblleft{}to hug, to embrace\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A avó abraçou os netos à chegada.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Grandma hugged her grandchildren when they arrived.}
\end{quote}

A hug is \emph{um abraço}; letters often end \emph{um abraço}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{abraçar} is inherited from Old Portuguese \emph{abraçar} (EtymDB), built on \emph{braço} \textquotedblleft{}arm\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{bracchium} \textquotedblleft{}arm\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
